title: Shareable-fact research: hooks, wording and sources
scope: Research and drafting only. No site source file was edited. Every hook below is phrased to the limit of a source that was actually opened and read during this research; anything that could not be opened is listed under couldNotVerify.
editorialRules: No exaggeration beyond what the cited record states.
Approximate or debated chronology stays approximate in the hook wording.
No museum endorsement is implied by citing a museum record.
No authentication advice: a test cut, a countermark or a weight is evidence to interpret, not a test a reader should apply.
'Mint State after 2,400 years' belongs to the single coin in src/one-owl.json (NGC 2086328-049) and must never be generalised to owls as a class.

hooks.hook: On the Acropolis in 408/7 BC, one owl was about four days' pay.
hooks.expansion: The building accounts for the Erechtheion record the wages of the people finishing the temple, and Attic Inscriptions Online summarises the rate they worked to: a day-wage of one drachma, or piece-rates worked out from it. A tetradrachm was four drachmas, so a single owl stood roughly for a four-day week of that work.
qualifications: Most surviving entries in the accounts are piece-rates for named tasks, not counted days; the one-drachma day-wage is AIO's summary of how the rates were computed, not a single quoted line.
The accounts cover one year of finishing work at one building, in the last years of the Peloponnesian War. They are not a wage series for the fifth century.
Nothing says a worker was actually handed a tetradrachm. The equivalence is arithmetic on the denomination, not a recorded payment.

hooks.hook: An Athenian law of 375/4 BC ordered that a fake owl be cut open on the spot and handed over to a goddess.
hooks.expansion: Nikophon's law put a public approver among the bankers' tables in the Agora and by the stele of Poseidon in Piraeus, and told him what to do with a coin that was not what it claimed. A piece with a bronze or lead core was to be cut through at once, and then became sacred property of the Mother of the Gods, deposited with the Council.
qualifications: The law is a document of 375/4 BC. It does not describe practice in every earlier or later year.
The clause on foreign silver struck with an Athenian type is partly restored; AIO records the restoration as plausible but notes the missing parallels. Do not build a claim on that clause.
This is a rule about what officials did, not a method a reader can use to judge a coin today.

hooks.hook: The owl on the Greek one-euro coin was copied from a fifth-century Athenian four-drachma coin.
hooks.expansion: The European Central Bank's record of the Greek national sides states the source of the design in plain words. The denomination changed, the metal changed, and the bird stayed.
qualifications: The ECB names a type, not a particular specimen. Do not claim the euro design copies any single museum coin, or any coin shown on this site.
'Copied from' is the ECB's own wording; keep it rather than upgrading it to a claim about artistic method.

hooks.hook: In 414 BC Aristophanes had a chorus of birds promise the judges owls that would nest in their purses and hatch small change.
hooks.expansion: In Birds the chorus offers the competition judges a bribe: the owls of Laurion will never run out on them, and will move in and breed. The joke only works because the audience heard the coin and the bird in the same word.
qualifications: This is a comic bribe aimed at the play's judges, not a report of monetary practice.

The Greek at line 1108 has the owls hatching out small change (mikra kermata); Eugene O'Neill's published English renders this as laying coins. Quote the published translation, or the Greek, rather than paraphrasing between them.
O'Neill's 1938 translation may still be in copyright. Link to Perseus and quote briefly; do not reproduce the passage at length.

hooks.hook: Athens found a design that worked and then left it alone until it stopped striking tetradrachms altogether.
hooks.expansion: The American Numismatic Society's chief curator, writing about the first owls, notes that the type spelled out its own origin so completely that the Athenians saw little need to change the basic design until tetradrachm production ended in the first century BC. Style shifted over those centuries; the idea of the coin did not.
qualifications: The claim is about the basic type, not about detail. Helmet ornament, eye rendering and style changed a great deal, which is what the coin families on this site are built on.
The explanation that the Peisistratids chose the type as a 'brand' for exported silver is reported by van Alfen as a current explanation, not asserted as fact. Keep it attributed and conditional.
This is a curator's public-facing post, not a peer-reviewed article.

hooks.hook: Some surviving owls carry a chisel cut: one in the American Numismatic Society, found in Egypt, is catalogued simply as 'One chisel cut'.
hooks.expansion: An archaic Athenian tetradrachm from the Asyut hoard is recorded at 17.047 g and worn, with a single chisel cut noted in its condition record. Cutting was also official business: the Athenian law of 375/4 BC required the city's approver to cut through any coin with a bronze or lead core.
qualifications: The ANS record states that this coin is cut. It does not say who cut it, when, where or why.
One catalogued specimen is not evidence for how common test cuts are; no reliable overall proportion was verified for this research.
A cut is evidence to interpret. Do not present it as a way of telling a genuine coin from a false one.

hooks.hook: Athens once decided not to share out a windfall of mine silver, and built a fleet with it instead.
hooks.expansion: Herodotus says the revenues from the mines at Laurium were about to be divided at ten drachmae a man when Themistocles persuaded the Athenians to build two hundred ships for the war with Aegina. The Athenaion Politeia tells it differently: a hundred-talent profit from newly found mines at Maronea, lent to the hundred richest Athenians, a hundred triremes, and the battle of Salamis.
qualifications: The two ancient accounts disagree on the mine, the number of ships and the mechanism. Present the disagreement rather than merging them.
Herodotus does not date the episode and does not connect these ships to Salamis; the Athenaion Politeia does. The conventional 483/2 BC comes from the archon year, not from either text.
Neither text mentions owls. Do not say the fleet was paid for in tetradrachms.
Godley's own footnote to Herodotus 7.144 observes that ten drachmae a head would come to far too small a sum to build 200 ships, and reads the passage as a contribution to a shipbuilding fund.
hooks.siteStatus: The site already tells the Laurion silver story in chapter 01 (the mining band, sources early-silver and mines), but it does not currently tell the Themistocles-and-the-fleet episode. This is genuinely new material, and it is supported.

hooks.hook: A 2025 survey of 999 coin hoards found Athenian coinage pushing well past the Greek world, into the Levant and Egypt.
hooks.expansion: Zane Mullins assembled 999 hoards and 160,007 coins from 550 to 300 BC to measure how Classical Greek coinages actually moved. Among the results the study singles out is the penetration of Athenian coinage into non-Greek areas such as the Levant and Egypt, alongside a count of the foreign imitations that followed it.
qualifications: Hoards record where coins were buried, not the routes they travelled or how they were used.
The sample covers 550-300 BC. It is not a statement about every period.
Some hoard descriptions do not separate Athenian coins from imitations; the study discusses imitations as a category of its own.

Flag 'the dollar of the ancient world' as popular framing. It appears in the headline of an ANS outreach post about the first owl, not as a claim argued in scholarly text, and no opened scholarly source used it.

hooks.hook: One owl was eight days on an Athenian jury.
hooks.expansion: The Athenaion Politeia lists what the city paid for public duties: half a drachma for the jury-courts, five obols for the Council, a drachma for an ordinary meeting of the Assembly. Four drachmas, the value of one tetradrachm, is eight days of jury pay.
qualifications: The Athenaion Politeia describes the arrangements of its own time, the later fourth century BC. It is not a rate that held for every year.
Its authorship is debated; it is transmitted under Aristotle's name.
Jury service was not daily employment, so eight days of pay is not eight days of life.
Rackham's 1952 translation may still be in copyright; link rather than reproduce at length.

hooks.hook: For a rower in the fleet that sailed for Sicily in 415 BC, one owl was four days at sea.
hooks.expansion: Thucydides says the treasury gave a drachma a day to each seaman of that expedition, and that the trierarchs added bounties of their own on top. At four drachmas, one tetradrachm covers four days of the state's share.
qualifications: This is the rate for one exceptionally well-funded expedition, which Thucydides presents as unusually lavish. It is not a standing naval wage.
Thucydides says captains paid extra, so what a man actually earned varied.
The related passage at 3.17.4, where hoplites at Potidaea draw two drachmae a day, is regarded by many editors as a later insertion; do not lead with it.

hooks.hook: When the Peloponnesian War began, Pericles told Athens it had six thousand talents of coined silver sitting on the Acropolis.
hooks.expansion: Thucydides reports the figure in Pericles' account of Athenian resources in 431 BC, and adds that the reserve had once stood at nine thousand seven hundred. On the standard Athenian accounting, six thousand talents is thirty-six million drachmas: the value of about nine million tetradrachms.
qualifications: The figure sits inside a speech that Thucydides reports, and modern historians debate it.
Thucydides says 'coined silver', not tetradrachms. The nine million figure is an illustration of scale, and is not a mintage estimate or a count of owls that existed.
The conversion depends on the accounting relation of 6,000 drachmas to the talent; cite it rather than leaving it implicit.
hooks.note: Strong 'wait, what?' value, but it carries two conversions. If the creator kit wants only clean single-step facts, hold this one back.

hooks.hook: On the Erechtheion accounts, the architect and the labourers were on the same day-wage.
hooks.expansion: Attic Inscriptions Online notes that the architect and the labourers, skilled and unskilled alike, were employed either on a day-wage of one drachma or on piece-rates computed from it. The building is one of the most refined on the Acropolis; the pay line is flat.
qualifications: This is AIO's editorial summary of the rates behind the accounts, not a quoted line of the inscription.
It describes one project in one year. Do not generalise it into a claim about Athenian wage structure.

hooks.hook: Some owls came back stamped by somebody other than Athens.
hooks.expansion: A classical Athenian tetradrachm in the American Numismatic Society, weighing 17.17 g, is recorded as countermarked. The mark is a later addition to a finished coin, made by a hand the record does not name.
qualifications: The record flags a countermark. It does not identify or locate the authority that applied it.
Do not attribute the mark to a named issuer, region or purpose on the strength of this record.
No opened source supported a general claim about 'Eastern countermarks' as a class; the reach sources cover circulation and imitation, not countermarking.
hooks.note: Weakest of the verified set. Usable as supporting detail beside the test-cut hook, not as a standalone shareable fact.

hooks.hook: Keep the site's existing wording: on this coin, theta is a circle with a central dot, the ancient counterpart of the printed theta.
hooks.expansion: The site already states this and cites the Open University's ancient Greek course, which compares dotted and crossed theta on Athenian ostraka. No stronger claim was verified.
qualifications: 'The dot inside the theta is a 2,400-year-old letterform' is not supportable as written. It implies a form still in use, and the dotted theta is older than the coin and was superseded, not carried forward into the printed letter.
The supporting source is a university course resource offering examples of Athenian writing. It is not a palaeographic authority and not a dating source for the coin.
No epigraphic authority on Attic letterforms could be opened for this research beyond that resource; Wikipedia was consulted only as a pointer and is not cited.
hooks.recommendation: Do not promote to the creator kit. Leave the existing artifact-story wording as it stands.

couldNotVerify.claim: The silver purity of Athenian tetradrachms, e.g. 'about 98% silver' or 'over 75% of owls are at least 98% silver'.
couldNotVerify.whatHappened: The relevant study is Davis, Gore, Sheedy & Albarede, 'Separating silver sources of Archaic Athenian coinage by comprehensive compositional analyses', Journal of Archaeological Science 114 (2020) 105068, doi:10.1016/j.jas.2019.105068. Its title, authors, journal and abstract were confirmed, and the abstract states that 788 coins were analysed by energy dispersive XRF. The abstract gives no purity figure. The open-access full text is hosted only on sciencedirect.com, which returned HTTP 403, and the HAL mirror returned a bot-protection page.
couldNotVerify.doNotUse: Any percentage figure for owl silver purity, and the claim that 86% of test-cut coins were over 98% silver. Both appeared only in search-engine summaries, not in a source that was opened.
couldNotVerify.howToResolve: Read the body of the 2020 JAS paper, or the companion piece 'Studies in Athenian Silver Coinage: Analysis of Archaic Owl Tetradrachms', MiN 6, 207-214, and quote the figure with its sample.

couldNotVerify.claim: How many owls Athens struck, in total or per year.
couldNotVerify.whatHappened: No mintage estimate from a museum, the ANS or a peer-reviewed source was located and opened. Die-study based estimates exist in the specialist literature but none was read.
couldNotVerify.howToResolve: The scale hook at rank 11 (Thucydides 2.13.3) gives a sourced sense of magnitude without claiming a mintage, and is the safe substitute.

couldNotVerify.claim: A proportion or frequency for test cuts among surviving owls.
couldNotVerify.whatHappened: Only dealer and hobbyist pages made quantitative claims. No museum, ANS or peer-reviewed statement of frequency was opened.
couldNotVerify.doNotUse: 'Most owls are test cut', or any percentage.
couldNotVerify.howToResolve: Cite the individual ANS specimen and the 375/4 BC law, which is what rank 6 does.

couldNotVerify.claim: Eastern countermarks on owls as a documented class, with issuing authorities.
couldNotVerify.whatHappened: An ANS collection record flagging a countermark was opened (1949.128.4), but no reputable source describing Eastern countermarking practice was opened. An ANS Pocket Change post on Attic tetradrachms in Persian-period Egypt proved to be about weight standards, not countermarks.
couldNotVerify.doNotUse: Any claim attributing countermarks to a named region, authority or purpose.
couldNotVerify.howToResolve: Consult van Alfen's published work on imitative owls, or an ANS hoard study, and cite the specific discussion.

couldNotVerify.claim: 'The dollar of the ancient world' as a scholarly characterisation.
couldNotVerify.whatHappened: The phrase 'the dollar of the ancient Greek world' was confirmed in the headline of an ANS Pocket Change post about the first Athenian owl. The body of that post is a video post and does not argue the claim. A phrase widely quoted online, 'one of the most widely used and widely circulating coinages of the ancient Greek world', was NOT found in the body of either ANS post when the pages were downloaded and searched directly. It appears to originate in search-engine summarisation.
couldNotVerify.doNotUse: That quoted sentence, attributed to the ANS or to van Alfen.
couldNotVerify.howToResolve: Use the Mullins 2025 abstract for reach, which is quantitative and quotable, and treat the dollar analogy as popular framing.

couldNotVerify.claim: Museum teaching resources on Athenian money that were located but not readable.
couldNotVerify.whatHappened: The Ashmolean Museum's 'Ancient Greek Coins: Notes for Teachers' PDF and the Attic Inscriptions Online A-level teachers' notes PDF were both downloaded but could not be converted to text; no PDF text-extraction tool is available in this environment.
couldNotVerify.howToResolve: Open both PDFs in a reader. The AIO notes are reported to state the obol/drachma/talent relations and would be a better citation than the University of Cincinnati teaching page used at rank 11.

sources.title: Erechtheion building accounts, 408/7 BC (IG I³ 476)
sources.author: Translation: Stephen Lambert & Robin Osborne; Attic Inscriptions Online
sources.scope: Wages and piece-rates on the Erechtheion. AIO's note 6 states that the architect and the labourers, both skilled and unskilled, were employed either on a day-wage of 1 dr. or on piece-rates computed on the basis of that wage.
sources.note: Most surviving entries record piece-rates for named tasks rather than counted days; the 1 dr. day-wage is AIO's editorial summary of the accounts, not a quoted line of the stone. The accounts cover one year of finishing work at one building.

sources.title: Athenian Constitution 62.2 (Athenaion Politeia)
sources.author: Aristotle; translation H. Rackham; Perseus Digital Library
sources.scope: State pay for public duties: a drachma for an ordinary meeting of the Assembly and a drachma and a half for a sovereign one, half a drachma for the jury-courts, five obols for the Council, and a drachma a day for the archon for Salamis.
sources.note: The Athenaion Politeia describes arrangements of its own time, the later fourth century BC, not a rate fixed for every year. Its authorship is debated; it is transmitted under Aristotle's name. Rackham's 1952 translation may remain in copyright: link rather than reproduce at length.

sources.title: History of the Peloponnesian War 6.31.3
sources.author: Thucydides; translation Richard Crawley; Perseus Digital Library
sources.scope: The Sicilian expedition of 415 BC: the treasury giving a drachma a day to each seaman, with the trierarchs adding bounties on top of the state's pay.
sources.note: A rate for one expedition that Thucydides presents as exceptionally costly, not a standing naval wage. Perseus publishes this translation under CC BY-SA 3.0 US.

sources.title: History of the Peloponnesian War 3.17.4
sources.author: Thucydides; translation Richard Crawley; Perseus Digital Library
sources.scope: Hoplites blockading Potidaea drawing two drachmae a day, one for the man himself and another for his servant.
sources.note: Many editors regard Thucydides 3.17 as a later insertion into the text and its figures as unreliable. Held in reserve; 6.31.3 is the safer pay citation.

sources.title: Birds 1106–1108
sources.author: Aristophanes; translation Eugene O'Neill, Jr.; Perseus Digital Library
sources.scope: The bird chorus promises the competition judges that the owls of Laurion will never fail them, that they will move in and nest in the judges' money-bags, and that they will hatch out small change.
sources.note: A comic bribe aimed at the play's judges, not a report of monetary practice. The Greek text is at Perseus text 1999.01.0025, same card; line 1108 reads ἐννεοττεύσουσι κἀκλέψουσι μικρὰ κέρματα. O'Neill's 1938 English may remain in copyright: link and quote briefly rather than reproducing the passage.

sources.title: The Histories 7.144
sources.author: Herodotus; translation A. D. Godley; Perseus Digital Library
sources.scope: Revenues from the mines at Laurium; a proposed distribution of ten drachmae a man; Themistocles persuading the Athenians to build two hundred ships instead, for the war with Aegina.
sources.note: Herodotus gives no year, names no coin type, and ties the ships to the Aeginetan war rather than to Salamis. Godley's own footnote calculates that ten drachmae a head would be far too small a sum to build two hundred ships and reads the passage as a contribution to a shipbuilding fund.

sources.title: Athenian Constitution 22.7 (Athenaion Politeia)
sources.author: Aristotle; translation H. Rackham; Perseus Digital Library
sources.scope: A hundred-talent profit from the newly discovered mines at Maronea; Themistocles has it lent to the hundred richest Athenians; a hundred triremes are built, and with these the Athenians fight the naval battle at Salamis.
sources.note: This account conflicts with Herodotus 7.144 on the mine, the number of ships and the mechanism. Rackham prints the archon's name as Nicomedes; the archon of 483/2 BC is usually printed Nikodemos. The conventional 483/2 BC date comes from the archon year, not from the text.

sources.title: History of the Peloponnesian War 2.13.3
sources.author: Thucydides; translation Richard Crawley; Perseus Digital Library
sources.scope: Pericles' account of Athenian resources in 431 BC: six thousand talents of coined silver in the Acropolis, out of nine thousand seven hundred that had once been there.
sources.note: A figure reported inside a speech, and one modern historians debate. Thucydides says coined silver, not tetradrachms, so any conversion to a number of owls illustrates scale and is not a mintage figure.

sources.title: The First Athenian Owls: Symbols of What, Exactly?
sources.author: Peter van Alfen · American Numismatic Society, Pocket Change
sources.scope: The civic legibility of the owl type and its longevity: the Athenians saw little need to change the basic design until they ceased minting tetradrachms completely in the first century BC.
sources.note: A curator's public-facing post, not a peer-reviewed article. The Peisistratid branding explanation is reported there as a current explanation rather than asserted. The claim concerns the basic type; style and detail changed considerably.

sources.title: Silver Tetradrachm, Athens, 515 BCE–482 BCE · 2008.39.34
sources.author: American Numismatic Society
sources.scope: A worn archaic Athenian tetradrachm, 17.047 g, 21 mm, recorded with one chisel cut and a secondary treatment of Cut, from the Asyut hoard (IGCH 1644).
sources.note: The record documents a cut on this specimen. It does not state who made the cut, when or why, and a single record is not evidence for how common test cuts are. Citing it implies no museum endorsement and offers no authentication guidance.

sources.title: Silver Tetradrachm, Athens, 450 BCE–400 BCE · 1949.128.4
sources.author: American Numismatic Society
sources.scope: A classical Athenian tetradrachm, 17.17 g, helmeted head of Athena right, ΑΘΕ with owl and olive spray in an incuse square, recorded with a secondary treatment of Countermarked, from hoard IGCH 1649.
sources.note: The record flags a countermark but does not identify or locate the countermarking authority. Do not attribute it to a named issuer, region or purpose on the strength of this record.

sources.title: Weights, Measures, Money
sources.author: Peter van Minnen · Department of Classics, University of Cincinnati
sources.scope: The accounting relations 1 drachma = 6 obols, 1 mina = 100 drachmas, 1 talent = 6000 drachmas.
sources.note: A teaching page, used here only for the accounting conversions. Its figure of 36 kg for the Attic talent is a commercial-weight figure and differs from the c. 26 kg usually given for the silver talent; do not cite it for weights. A museum or AIO statement of the same relations would be a stronger citation if one can be opened.

sources.title: The ANS's Greatest Coins: the first Athenian “Owl”. The dollar of the ancient Greek world
sources.author: Peter van Alfen · American Numismatic Society, Pocket Change
sources.scope: Record of where the phrase “the dollar of the ancient Greek world” actually comes from: the headline of an ANS video post about the first Athenian owl.
sources.note: Held as evidence about the phrasing, not as support for a claim. The analogy is a headline on a video post and is not argued in the body text. Treat it as popular framing attributable to ANS outreach, never as a research finding.

reusedExistingSources.verifiedThisSession: Nikophon's law, 375/4 BC: the approver sits among the tables in the Agora (lines 4-5) and by the stele of Poseidon in Piraeus (lines 36-41); a coin with a bronze or lead core is cut through immediately and becomes sacred property of the Mother of the Gods, deposited with the Council (lines 10-13). The foreign-coin clause remains a restoration.
The ECB's Greek national-sides page states that the owl on the €1 design was copied from an ancient Athenian 4-drachma coin of the fifth century BC.

Mullins 2025, Economic History Review. The abstract states a sample of 999 hoards and 160,007 coins from 550 to 300 BC, and singles out the penetration of Athenian coinage into non-Greek areas such as the Levant and Egypt, with foreign imitations quantified separately.
Used only for the denomination: a tetradrachm is four drachmas. Already carried in the site glossary.
Not re-verified beyond the site's existing record; no stronger letterform authority could be opened.
